newsitem.title: JAPAN: Turmoil seen looming for Japan minority government.
newsitem.headline: Turmoil seen looming for Japan minority government.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was like a runner stalled in the starting blocks looking at a growing line of high hurdles to clear when he launched Japan's 1997 parliamentary session on Monday.

Rebels were in the 35th day of holding hostages at the Japanese embassy in Peru, the country's worst-ever oil spill was getting bigger and financial markets greeted a policy speech promising "wisdom and boldness" with a 3.37 percent fall in the stock market.

Even on the eve of the speech, a weekend survey of voters by the private Fuji television network showed 76.4 percent thought the Hashimoto government would make no headway in its main aims of cutting government red tape and implementing economic reforms.
Political analysts see no relief on the horizon, predicting a crisis every three months this year.
The root of the predictions is simple mathematics.
Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party goes into 1997 eleven seats shy of a majority in the 500-seat Lower House.
With many testing issues ahead, the prime minister and his party are always vulnerable to switches in allegiance which could bring either the man, or the party, down.

Although the opposition appears too disorganised at this stage to mount an immediate serious challenge to the LDP minority government, political analysts say Hashimoto's year of living dangerously is likely to start as early as March.
The government, formed after the conservative LDP fell short of a majority in October polls, relies on the 17 votes of the Social Democratic Party and the tiny Sakigake party.
The parties were full members of a three-party coalition formed in 1994 and headed by Hashimoto for the past year.
But for this session of parliament they have opted out of the cabinet, and could go their own way on the fiscal 1997/98 budget scheduled to be voted on by the end of March.
The parties can also break the Hashimoto government's plan to pass a 2.67 trillion yen ($22.8 billion) supplementary budget for 1996/97 by its self-imposed January 31 deadline.

The Social Democrats are so far sitting on the fence on the supplementary budget, but Sakigake has joined opposition to an extra spending plan, which critics say is heavy with post-election pork barrel spending.
Asked about a "March crisis" sparked by the two parties, cabinet spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama acknowledged the administration was "in a risky situation".
"If other parties move to topple the cabinet, they may find it possible," he told reporters on Monday.

Even if Hashimoto navigates the two budgets through parliament, a fresh conflict is set to erupt over Okinawa in May with the expiration of contracts for land forcibly leased by the government for 12 U.S. military bases on the island.
A heavy-handed Okinawa policy by the LDP, such as forcing through parliament special bills to renew the leases, would likely alienate the Social Democrats leading them to walk out of the coalition.
Smouldering in the background all the time are also government corruption scandals, a perennial feature of LDP rule and a main weapon in the opposition parties' arsenal.

Investigations into a scandal which broke last year at the health ministry, resulting in the arrests of businessmen and senior bureaucrats on bribery allegations, are set to conclude before Parliament ends on June 18.
Another scandal involves an Osaka oil dealer with close ties to top trade ministry officials.
Come September, if Hashimoto has fared badly in his previous tests, things could really hot up when he faces an election for his post as leader of the LDP.
